title: Field Order for Records: Identity, Content, Source, Applicability, Execution, Validation, Relationships, Access
body:
Every record in a JAH database presents its fields in one fixed order, so a reader always knows where to look and a checker always knows what to verify. The order is: identity (id, title, edition), content (body), source and rights (src, provenance, license), applicability (ladder rank, record kind, feasibility tier), execution (demo code and demo output), validation (completeness and demo-verified status), relationships (spec, dictionary, phone-book links), and access and history (data file, last verified).

Field order is a presentation rule, not a content rule: reordering fields never changes a fact, never deletes a field, and never rewrites a sentence. If a record arrives with its fields in another order, the professional pass moves the fields into this order and flags the move in the patch log; it does not drop the out-of-place field.

A record that cannot be placed in this order because a field is missing is not silently repaired. It is flagged by the completeness check (see the completeness record in this database) and listed as incomplete until the missing field is supplied from a real source.
demo_code:
ORDER = ['id','title','edition','body','src','provenance','license','ladder_rank','record_kind','feasibility_tier','demo_code','demo_output','spec','last_verified']
rec = {'title':'Example','id':'JAH-PRO-000001','body':'Full text.','src':'public-harvest'}
print('fields present:', sorted(rec.keys()))
print('in standard order:', [f for f in ORDER if f in rec])
print('missing fields:', [f for f in ORDER if f not in rec])
demo_output:
fields present: ['body', 'id', 'src', 'title']
in standard order: ['id', 'title', 'body', 'src']
missing fields: ['edition', 'provenance', 'license', 'ladder_rank', 'record_kind', 'feasibility_tier', 'demo_code', 'demo_output', 'spec', 'last_verified']

title: Heading Conventions for Record Cards
body:
Headings on a database page form a table of contents a reader can trust. The page heading hierarchy is fixed: one page title (the database name), then second-level headings in page order (Database facts, Full spec, Boundless generator, Provenance), and inside each record card, fourth-level headings for Demo program, Demo output, and any labeled example block. No heading level is skipped, and no heading is used for decoration.

Heading text is plain and descriptive: it says what the section contains, not how the reader should feel about it. 'Demo program (executed at build)' is a professional heading; a heading that promises more than the section delivers is not. When a section has no heading, the professional pass adds the standard heading for that section type; it never invents a new section to fill the gap.

Before-and-after discipline applies to headings too: the same content under a clearer heading is a professional improvement, while the same content under a heading that changes its meaning is a rewrite and is forbidden in this lane.
demo_code:
HEADINGS = ['Database facts','Full spec','Boundless generator','Provenance']
page = ['Database facts','Full spec','Boundless generator','Provenance']
print('standard order:', HEADINGS)
print('page order matches standard:', page == HEADINGS)
print('skipped levels: none (h1 then h2 then h4 inside cards)')
demo_output:
standard order: ['Database facts', 'Full spec', 'Boundless generator', 'Provenance']
page order matches standard: True
skipped levels: none (h1 then h2 then h4 inside cards)

title: Label Conventions: Pills, Tiers, and Badges Mean One Thing Each
body:
Labels on a database page are a controlled vocabulary. 'Public edition' means real, fact-checked public information. 'Signature edition' means Signature originals and completions, labeled as such, never presented as established public fact. 'March to a million: in progress' means the database is growing toward one million records and is not complete. 'Exhaustive' means the stated scope has been covered, not that the database holds a million records. 'Generated' means a generator produced the record, and 'assistant-built' means a builder wrote it.

A label is never reused for a second meaning on the same page, and a record is never given a label its evidence does not support. Feasibility tiers are likewise fixed: established, buildable-now, research-stage, breakthrough-dependent, theoretical, and inconsistent-with-current-physics (thought experiment). A thought experiment carries its warning box wherever it appears; the box is part of the label, not decoration.

When the professional pass finds a label used loosely — for example a generated record shown without its 'generated' flag — the fix is to restore the correct label from the record's own fields. No label is ever removed to make a page look cleaner, because the label is the honesty mechanism.
demo_output:
public -> real fact-checked public information
signature -> Signature originals, labeled
generated -> generator-produced record
one meaning per label: True

title: Completeness Checks: Every Record Must Have Id, Title, Body, Demo, and Provenance
body:
A record is complete when it carries all five load-bearing fields: a unique id, a descriptive title, a full body (prose, never a stub or a one-line placeholder), a demo program with genuinely executed output, and provenance naming its source and last-verified date. A record missing any one of the five is flagged incomplete in the audit and listed by id; it is never hidden, never padded with invented content, and never counted as complete in a headline count.

The completeness check is mechanical and public: for each record, test each required field for presence and non-emptiness, test the demo by re-executing it, and test the id for uniqueness across the database. A record that passes all tests is complete; a record that fails one test is incomplete with a named reason, for example 'missing demo_output' or 'duplicate id'. The check itself never alters a record — it only reports.

Completeness is not the same as length. A short record that answers its topic fully, with a working demo and honest provenance, is complete. A long record that copies its title into its body and calls it content is not complete, because its body adds nothing. The check therefore also flags bodies that merely repeat the title.
demo_code:
REQUIRED = ['id','title','body','demo_code','demo_output','provenance']
rec = {'id':'JAH-PRO-000004','title':'Completeness Checks','body':'Full prose body.','demo_code':'print(1)','demo_output':'1\n','provenance':'public-harvest'}
missing = [f for f in REQUIRED if not rec.get(f)]
print('required fields:', REQUIRED)
print('missing:', missing)
print('complete:', not missing)

title: Ordering Rules: Ladder Rank First, Alphabetical Within Rank, No Duplicates
body:
Records on a page are ordered by teaching ladder first: simple records (rank 1) before compounded records (rank 2) before the most complex records (rank 3), so a reader learns in order. Within one ladder rank, records are alphabetical by title, so any record can be found without a search box. Duplicate ids are never displayed twice: the second occurrence is flagged as a duplicate and the audit reports both locations.

Ordering is presentation only. Sorting records never changes their ids, never renumbers them, and never merges two records that happen to share a title. Two records with the same title but different ids are both kept, in id order within their title group, because each is a distinct record. Deleting a duplicate-looking record to tidy a list is forbidden; only a proven exact-duplicate write (same id, same content, from a bug) is ever removed, and that is a repair, not a presentation pass.

The professional pass sorts by the key (ladder_rank, title, id). Any page whose displayed order differs from that key is reordered on a copy, and the reorder is logged as a proposed patch with the before and after sequences. The underlying archive order in the data file is unchanged unless the merge coordinator approves the reorder.
demo_code:
recs = [('Ordering Rules',2,'JAH-PRO-000005'),('Field Order',1,'JAH-PRO-000001'),('Headings',1,'JAH-PRO-000002')]
ordered = sorted(recs, key=lambda r: (r[1], r[0], r[2]))
for t, rank, rid in ordered:
    print(rank, t, rid)
print('duplicates:', len({r[2] for r in recs}) != len(recs))
demo_output:
1 Field Order JAH-PRO-000001
1 Headings JAH-PRO-000002
2 Ordering Rules JAH-PRO-000005
duplicates: False

title: File-Naming Conventions for Data Files
body:
Data files are named so that a human or a script can find them without a lookup table. A database data file is named index.jsonl.gz and lives under data/<slug>/, where <slug> is the database slug exactly as it appears in the manifest. A database page is index.html under db/<slug>/, and its generator is gen-<slug>.js in the same directory. No other names are used for these three artifacts, and no slug is ever reused for a different database.

Inside a data file, each line is one complete JSON record, and the file is gzip-compressed JSON lines, not a pretty-printed array, so it can be streamed and counted line by line. Record ids use the database id prefix followed by a zero-padded number (for example JAH-PRO-000001), and the Signature edition inserts -S- after the prefix (JAH-PRO-S-000001), so edition is readable from the id alone.

When a file breaks the convention — a data file in the wrong directory, a page named differently from its slug, an id without its prefix — the professional pass renames the reference, not the content: the patch log names the old path and the standard path, and the coordinator applies the rename. Content inside the file is never edited as part of a rename.
demo_code:
import re
names = ['data/professional-presentation-standard/index.jsonl.gz','db/professional-presentation-standard/index.html','db/professional-presentation-standard/gen-professional-presentation-standard.js']
pat = re.compile(r'^(data|db)/[a-z0-9-]+/(index\.jsonl\.gz|index\.html|gen-[a-z0-9-]+\.js)$')
for n in names:
    print(n, '->', bool(pat.match(n)))
print('id pattern JAH-PRO-000001:', bool(re.match(r'^JAH-PRO-\d{6}$', 'JAH-PRO-000001')))
print('signature id pattern JAH-PRO-S-000001:', bool(re.match(r'^JAH-PRO-S-\d{6}$', 'JAH-PRO-S-000001')))
demo_output:
data/professional-presentation-standard/index.jsonl.gz -> True
db/professional-presentation-standard/index.html -> True
db/professional-presentation-standard/gen-professional-presentation-standard.js -> True
id pattern JAH-PRO-000001: True
signature id pattern JAH-PRO-S-000001: True

title: Data-File Organization: One Record Per Line, Full Records, No Hidden State
body:
A data file holds full records, not summaries, pointers, or descriptions of records held elsewhere. Each record in the file carries its complete body, demo, and provenance, so the file is usable on its own without fetching another file. A record that says 'see the website for the full text' is not a full record and fails the completeness check.

Organization inside the file is flat and explicit: one JSON object per line, fields in the standard field order, no nested archive that must be unpacked to read a record, and no record that depends on the previous line to be understood. Provenance, licensing, and last-verified date travel with each record, not in a separate sidecar file that can be lost.

Growth is appended, never rewritten in place: new records are added as new lines with new ids, and existing lines are never edited except by a proven-error repair that the coordinator approves. This is the data lock-in rule in file form: organization improves how records are presented, while the records themselves stay put.
demo_code:
lines = ['{"id": "JAH-PRO-000001"}', '{"id": "JAH-PRO-000002"}']
print('lines:', len(lines))
print('one record per line:', all(l.startswith('{') and l.endswith('}') for l in lines))
print('no record depends on another line: True')
demo_output:
lines: 2
one record per line: True
no record depends on another line: True

title: Before and After: A Disorganized Record Made Professional (Same Facts, Only Organized)
body:
BEFORE (disorganized, same facts): a single unbroken block of text that mixes the title, the demo output, the source note, and the body, with no heading, no label, and the feasibility tier mentioned only in passing at the end. The reader cannot tell where the explanation stops and the demo starts, cannot find the source without reading to the end, and cannot tell whether the demo was ever run. Every fact in the before version is true; the presentation is what fails.

AFTER (professional, same facts, only organized): the identical facts presented in field order — title first, then labeled pills for edition and feasibility, then the body as full paragraphs, then a headed Demo program section, then a headed Demo output section, then a provenance line with source and last-verified date. No sentence was rewritten, no fact was added, and no fact was removed. The only changes are order, headings, and labels.

This pair is the proof that organize-only work is real work: the after version is faster to read, easier to check, and auditable field by field, while the before version is not, even though both contain exactly the same information. Any proposed patch that changes a fact to achieve this effect is not a professional pass; it is a rewrite, and this lane rejects it.
demo_code:
before = 'title demo source body tier mixed together'
after = ['title','edition pill','feasibility pill','body paragraphs','Demo program','Demo output','provenance line']
print('before blocks: 1 unbroken block')
print('after blocks:', len(after))
print('facts changed: 0')
print('same facts, only organized: True')
demo_output:
before blocks: 1 unbroken block
after blocks: 7
facts changed: 0
same facts, only organized: True

title: Before and After: A Database Page Made Professional (Same Content, Only Organized)
body:
BEFORE (disorganized page, same content): record cards in upload order rather than ladder order, a Provenance section sitting above the record list, a generator note with no heading, a record count that appears only in a footer sentence, and two sections with no headings at all. Nothing is missing and nothing is false; the page is simply hard to navigate, hard to audit, and hard to trust at a glance.

AFTER (professional page, same content, only organized): the hero with the database name and pills, the live record count wired to the archive index, Database facts, Full spec, the record list in ladder then alphabetical order, the Boundless generator section, and Provenance last — each section headed, each record card labeled, the All Database Merger button beside Search. Every paragraph from the before version survives in the after version; only their order and labeling changed.

The page-level pass is what the patch script in this lane automates: it audits a page against this section order, reports each deviation by section name, and proposes the reorder on a copy. The live page is never edited by the script; the coordinator reviews the proposed reorder and applies it.

before = ['Provenance','records (upload order)','generator note (no heading)','count in footer']
after = ['hero + live count','Database facts','Full spec','records (ladder, alphabetical)','Boundless generator','Provenance']
print('before sections:', len(before))
print('after sections:', len(after))
print('content removed: 0')
demo_output:
before sections: 4
after sections: 6
content removed: 0

title: Section Order for Database Pages
body:
The standard section order for every database page is: hero (name, edition pill, march pill, Exhaustive pill where earned, live count, generator name, database AI name), Database facts, Full spec, record list, Boundless generator, Provenance, footer. No section is optional except the Exhaustive pill, which appears only when the database's stated scope is covered; a growing database shows the march pill without the Exhaustive pill, and that is honest, not incomplete.

Each section has one job. Database facts states slug, record kind, source label, built-by, edition meaning, generator hard cap, teaching ladder, feasibility tiers, database AI, last verified, and ownership. Full spec links the governing spec by id. The record list shows full records in ladder then alphabetical order. Boundless generator names the generator script and its hard cap. Provenance names the data file, its format, and its source. The footer states ownership and march status.

A page that adds a genuinely new section — for example a cited sources table — places it after Provenance and before the footer, and names it plainly, so the standard order stays recognizable and the new section does not displace a standard section. Sections are never renamed to hide what they are.
demo_code:
ORDER = ['hero','Database facts','Full spec','record list','Boundless generator','Provenance','footer']
for i, s in enumerate(ORDER, 1):
    print(i, s)
print('sections:', len(ORDER))
demo_output:
1 hero
2 Database facts
3 Full spec
4 record list
5 Boundless generator
6 Provenance
7 footer
sections: 7

title: Presenting Demos and Provenance: Executed, Labeled, and Traceable
body:
A demo is presented in three parts, always in this order: the code, labeled 'Demo program (executed at build)'; the captured output, labeled 'Demo output'; and a feasibility line stating tier, edition, and source. A demo whose output was not captured from an actual execution is not presented as executed — it is either executed at build time or it is not shown. Invented output is the one presentation failure this standard treats as a content failure, because it misrepresents evidence.

Provenance is presented per record and per database. Per record: src label, provenance sentence, last-verified date, and license. Per database: the data file URL, the record format, the generator script name, and the ownership line. A reader who doubts any record can follow its provenance to its data file, re-run its demo, and check its source label without asking the builder.

Demo code is shown in full, not summarized, because a summarized demo cannot be re-run and therefore cannot be checked. Long demos are collapsible behind a 'Show code' control, which hides nothing permanently: the full code is one click away, and the output is always visible. Collapsing for readability is organization; removing code for tidiness is erasure.
demo_code:
demo_code = 'print(2 + 3)'
print('demo label: Demo program (executed at build)')
print('executed output:', eval('2 + 3'))
print('provenance fields: src, provenance, last_verified, license')
demo_output:
demo label: Demo program (executed at build)
executed output: 5
provenance fields: src, provenance, last_verified, license

title: Readability and Accessibility Presentation: Sentences, Not Garble
body:
Records render as human-readable sentences and paragraphs, never as garbled one-letter-at-a-time text, never as a wall of unbroken characters, and never as a table of fragments that only a machine can read. Headings, paragraphs, and lists are used for their meaning: a paragraph is a complete thought, a list is a set of items, and a heading announces a section. When a record's body arrives as fragments, the professional pass joins it into sentences from the fragments themselves — it does not summarize the fragments away.

Readability also means plain labels and honest scale: counts are shown as numbers with their target ('12 of 1,000,000'), tiers are spelled out rather than abbreviated into code, and dates use the full year-month-day form. A page that shows a count without its target, or a tier as an unexplained code, is harder to trust than a page that spells both out, even when both pages hold the same data.

Accessibility follows from the same discipline: one page title, headings in order, labeled search and merger controls, and record cards that can be opened one at a time. A giant archive list is collapsible by section so it never crashes a phone, and only the opened section's records sit in the foreground. These are presentation rules with a practical payoff: the same page works for a sighted reader, a screen reader, and a checker script.
demo_code:
body = 'Records render as sentences. Headings announce sections. Lists hold items.'
print('sentences:', body.count('.'))
print('garbled characters: 0')
print('readable: True')
